title: Atomics and compare-and-set
goal: By the end you can write a compare-and-set retry loop, choose between `AtomicLong`, `LongAdder` and `AtomicReference`, and explain why two atomic calls in a row are not atomic.
opening:
Picture the bank's busiest account on payday. Eight tellers, each a thread (one line of work among several in the program), add deposits to its balance at once. In Race conditions: why count++ lies, a plain `long` field lost more than two thirds of those deposits. That lesson fixed a counter with an `AtomicInteger`, a number whose updates happen in one step that no other thread can split. It promised to open the atomic up later, and this lesson keeps that promise.

Every lock in the last lesson made threads wait in line for a key, even the ones that could give up. An atomic number keeps no line at all. A thread that loses a race shrugs and tries again, a few nanoseconds (billionths of a second) later.

That speed is easy to mistake for safety. A withdrawal that checks `balance.get()` and then calls `balance.addAndGet(-cents)` uses two perfectly atomic calls, and it can still take the account below zero.

In this lesson, we'll open the atomic up, build any update from one instruction and a loop, count a busy day's deposits, and move money between two balances at once. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: `balance` is an `AtomicLong` holding 100. Two threads run `if (balance.get() >= 80) balance.addAndGet(-80);` at the same moment. What can the balance end at?
options: Only 20: `AtomicLong` makes the whole line thread-safe
20 or 100, because one of the two updates can be lost
20 or -60: both threads can pass the check before either takes the money
Only -60, because both checks always run first
warmup.why: Each call is atomic on its own, so no update is lost: whatever `addAndGet` does, it does completely. But the check and the withdrawal are two calls with a gap between them. Both threads can see 100, both decide there's enough, and both take 80. That's check-then-act from Race conditions: why count++ lies, built out of atomic parts. The worked example puts the check inside one compare-and-set.

sections.h: One step nobody can split: what an atomic variable does
sections.body:
Let's start with the balance itself. Here it is as an `AtomicLong`, with a deposit and a read:

```java
private final AtomicLong balanceCents = new AtomicLong();   // no lock needed

void deposit(long cents) {
    balanceCents.addAndGet(cents);        // read, add, write: one step nobody can split
}

long balance() {
    return balanceCents.get();            // like a volatile read: sees the latest value
}
```

```kotlin
private val balanceCents = AtomicLong()      // no lock needed

fun deposit(cents: Long) {
    balanceCents.addAndGet(cents)            // read, add, write: one step nobody can split
}

fun balance(): Long = balanceCents.get()     // like a volatile read: sees the latest value
```

An **atomic variable** holds one value and offers read-modify-write operations (read the value, change it, write it back, as `count++` does) that no other thread can split. `addAndGet` reads, adds and writes as one step. Its `get()` and `set()` behave like reads and writes of a `volatile` field, a field whose reads always see the latest write from any thread.

The method names tell you what comes back. `incrementAndGet()` returns the new value, and `getAndIncrement()` returns the old one. The same pairs exist for add, update and accumulate. `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicLong`, `AtomicBoolean` and `AtomicReference` cover most needs.

How does a library turn three steps into one without a lock? It asks the processor. On x86 processors, the kind in most laptops and servers, HotSpot (the standard JVM) compiles `addAndGet` to a single `lock xadd` instruction, and `compareAndSet` to `lock cmpxchg`. ARM64 processors have their own equivalents. While that instruction runs, the core keeps the variable's cache line to itself. A cache line is the small block of memory that a core copies into its own fast memory, its cache. A core must own the line before it can write to it. So no other core can get in between the read and the write.

No thread ever waits for another. If the operating system pauses a thread, that thread is never in the middle of an atomic update: the instruction either happened or it didn't. So some thread always makes progress, which is what **lock-free** means. A lock, the guard that lets one thread in at a time, is different. A thread that is paused while it holds a lock stops every thread that needs it, just as the interest job stopped the cash machine in the last lesson.

Predict from the mechanism. In the middle of payday, the operating system pauses teller 3 for 50 ms. With the `AtomicLong`, what do the other seven tellers do in those 50 ms? And with a lock that teller 3 held at that moment? (With the atomic, they keep depositing: teller 3 was paused before or after its instruction, never inside it. With the lock, all seven wait the full 50 ms.)

Atomics have one hard limit, and it's the one from the opening. Each atomic protects one variable, one call at a time. Two calls in a row are two steps with a gap between them, and the warm-up's withdrawal lives in that gap. It checks, then acts on what it saw, a shape called check-then-act. To close it, we need the operation underneath all the others.

aside.title: If atomics need no lock, why is the instruction called lock xadd?
aside.body: The `lock` there is a prefix on one processor instruction, not a Java lock. It tells the core to hold on to the variable's cache line until that one instruction is done. No thread ever joins a line for it, the way threads wait for a `ReentrantLock`, and the hold ends a few nanoseconds later. Other cores that want the same line do stall for those nanoseconds, though. That small stall, repeated millions of times, is the cost the `LongAdder` section measures.

sections.h: Letting the library write the loop: updateAndGet, and a function that runs twice
sections.body:
`updateAndGet(f)` and `accumulateAndGet(x, f)` contain the loop:

```java
max.accumulateAndGet(amount, Math::max);          // the max tracker's loop, written for you
balanceCents.updateAndGet(b -> b + 100);          // any pure function of the old value
```

```kotlin
max.accumulateAndGet(amount, Math::max)           // the max tracker's loop, written for you
balanceCents.updateAndGet { b -> b + 100 }        // any pure function of the old value
```

Inside, they read the value, call your function, and try the CAS. When the CAS fails, they call your function again with the new value. So your function can run more than once for one update, and the results of the extra runs are thrown away.

Let's count them. `UpdateTwice` starts four threads together, and each makes 250,000 one-cent deposits with `updateAndGet`. The function also counts how often it runs. Guess before you look: exactly 1,000,000 times?

```text
updates: 1,000,000   times the function ran: 1,294,839
```

The balance is exact, and the function ran 294,839 more times than there were deposits. Each extra run was a lost race whose result was thrown away. In six runs here, the extra runs came to between 29 and 99 percent of the deposits, so the number depends on how hard the threads collide. If that function had texted the customer, the bank would have sent close to 300,000 extra texts, for deposits that each happened once.

So the function must be **pure**: it looks only at its input and returns a result. No logging, no counters, no messages, no reads of other shared data that might change. Do any side effects after the call returns, using the value it returned.

**The update function may run more than once. Keep it pure, and act on the value it returns.**

The `get` variants, `getAndUpdate` and `getAndAccumulate`, return the value from before the update. Use them when the caller needs to know whether its own update applied. The worked example uses exactly that to build a withdrawal that never overdraws.

Every CAS so far fought over one variable. On a busy day, that fight is the cost.

sections.h: Counting on a busy day: LongAdder for statistics, AtomicLong for decisions
sections.body:
The fight has a name: **contention**, many threads trying to change the same thing at the same moment. Here's a place it bites. The manager's screen shows how many deposits the bank has taken today. Eight threads add to that count all day, and someone glances at it now and then. On one `AtomicLong`, that's one cache line that every core wants at once. Each increment pulls the line over to its own core, and the cores spend their time passing it around.

`LongAdder` (JDK 8) spreads the count over several cells, small counters of their own. When threads collide on one cell, it moves them to different cells, so they mostly write to different cache lines. `sum()` adds the base value and all the cells together:

```java
private final LongAdder depositsToday = new LongAdder();

void onDeposit() { depositsToday.increment(); }          // threads mostly hit different cells
long depositsSoFar() { return depositsToday.sum(); }     // adds the cells up: not a snapshot
```

```kotlin
private val depositsToday = LongAdder()

fun onDeposit() = depositsToday.increment()               // threads mostly hit different cells
fun depositsSoFar(): Long = depositsToday.sum()           // adds the cells up: not a snapshot
```

`AdderVsAtomic` races the two. Eight threads count 2,000,000 deposits each, first on one `AtomicLong`, then on a `LongAdder`. I guessed the adder would win by a few times. One run printed:

```text
round 1: AtomicLong 16,000,000 in  669 ms   LongAdder 16,000,000 in   92 ms
round 2: AtomicLong 16,000,000 in  482 ms   LongAdder 16,000,000 in   71 ms
round 3: AtomicLong 16,000,000 in  578 ms   LongAdder 16,000,000 in   53 ms
```

Correctness first: both counted all 16,000,000. Then speed: the `LongAdder` was 7 to 11 times faster, more than I guessed. With a single thread the gap shrinks or disappears, because there's no contention for the adder to avoid.

The price is in `sum()`. It reads the cells one by one while other threads keep adding. Its Javadoc (the official API documentation) says plainly that the result is not an atomic snapshot: increments made during the sum might not be counted. The adder also uses more memory than one `long`.

That gives a clean rule. Use `LongAdder` for statistics that many threads update and someone reads now and then: deposits taken, requests served, payments refused. Use `AtomicLong` when the value drives a decision, such as a balance that must not go below zero, a sequence number, or a limit. A decision needs the exact current value and a compare-and-set against it, and `LongAdder` has neither. `LongAccumulator` does the same trick for other functions, such as a maximum, with the same caveat on reads.

**Count with a LongAdder. Decide with an AtomicLong.**

One number at a time, then. A transfer changes two.

sections.h: Two balances in one swap: AtomicReference, and the ABA trap

try.title: Play out ABA by hand
steps: Read `AbaDemo`. It plays both threads on one thread, step by step, so the bad order of events happens every time. Nodes are recycled.
Before you run it, predict the stack after T1's `compareAndSet`.
Run it and compare the plain `AtomicReference` with the `AtomicStampedReference`.

code.title: AbaDemo.java

alt.title: AbaDemo.kt
alt.src:
package workbench.concurrency.l08

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicStampedReference

// The ABA problem, played out by hand on one thread so it happens every time.
// Nodes are recycled (mutable next), as in a pooled or off-heap structure.
private class AbaNode(val name: String, var next: AbaNode?)

private fun show(start: AbaNode?): String =
    generateSequence(start) { it.next }.joinToString(" -> ") { it.name }.ifEmpty { "(empty)" }

fun main() {
    val c = AbaNode("C", null)
    val b = AbaNode("B", c)
    val a = AbaNode("A", b)

    val head = AtomicReference(a)
    println("start:                   ${show(head.get())}")
    val top = head.get()
    val next = top.next                                           // T1 starts a pop...
    println("T1 reads top=A, next=B, then is paused")
    head.set(b)                                                   // T2 pops A
    head.set(c)                                                   // T2 pops B (B is now T2's)
    a.next = head.get()
    head.set(a)                                                   // T2 pushes the recycled A
    println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: ${show(head.get())}")
    val ok = head.compareAndSet(top, next)                        // T1 resumes: head is A again
    println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B) = $ok")
    println("stack now:               ${show(head.get())}   (B was popped by T2: corrupted)")

    println()
    a.next = b; b.next = c
    val stamped = AtomicStampedReference(a, 0)
    val stampHolder = IntArray(1)
    val top2 = stamped.get(stampHolder)                           // T1 reads the node AND the stamp
    val stamp = stampHolder[0]
    val next2 = top2.next
    println("T1 reads top=A, stamp=$stamp, next=B, then is paused")
    stamped.set(b, 1)                                             // every change bumps the stamp
    stamped.set(c, 2)
    a.next = c
    stamped.set(a, 3)
    println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: stamp is now ${stamped.stamp}")
    val ok2 = stamped.compareAndSet(top2, next2, stamp, stamp + 1)
    println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B, stamp $stamp) = $ok2, so T1 re-reads and retries")
}

try.expect: With the plain reference, T1's `compareAndSet(A, B)` returns `true` and the stack becomes `B -> C`, although T2 had already popped B: the stack is corrupted. With the stamp, the same CAS returns `false`, because the stamp moved from 0 to 3, so T1 reads again and retries.

compare.title: A max tracker with Java's atomics and Kotlin's

java.title: Java (java.util.concurrent.atomic)

kotlin.title: Kotlin (kotlin.concurrent.atomics)

compare.note: On the JVM, most Kotlin code simply uses `java.util.concurrent.atomic`, and everything in this lesson works the same from Kotlin. Kotlin 2.1 added its own atomics in `kotlin.concurrent.atomics`, mainly for code that must also run outside the JVM. The names differ (`load`, `fetchAndAdd`, `update`), and in the Kotlin 2.4 standard library they are still marked experimental, so they need `@OptIn(ExperimentalAtomicApi::class)`. Underneath, on the JVM, they are the same compare-and-set. One thing doesn't change between the languages: `@Volatile var count = 0` followed by `count++` compiles happily in Kotlin and loses updates exactly like the Java version.

worked.title: A withdrawal that never overdraws, without a lock

steps.say: An account must never go below zero. `tryWithdraw` should take the money only if there's enough, and many threads call it at once. Here's a first attempt with an `AtomicLong`. Look for the race before reading on.

Each call on `balanceCents` is atomic. The pair isn't: with 100 in the account, two threads can both pass the check for 80, and both take it, ending at -60. Making the variable atomic didn't make the logic atomic. The check has to happen inside the compare-and-set.
The CAS loop checks the very value it is about to replace. If another thread changes the balance in between, the CAS fails and the loop decides again on fresh data.

The same thing with `getAndUpdate`. The function is pure: it looks only at `b`. Before reading the next step, explain to yourself why the second line checks `before >= cents`, instead of checking whether the value changed.

`getAndUpdate` returns the value that its last, successful run of the function saw. If that value covered `cents`, the function took the money, so this caller's withdrawal went through. If it didn't, the function returned `b` unchanged and nothing was taken. Checking whether the value changed tells you nothing, because other threads change it all the time. This is also why `LongAdder` is the wrong tool for a balance: it has no compare-and-set, and its `sum()` isn't exact while others add. If you keep balances in a database, the same idea becomes one statement, `UPDATE account SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ?`, followed by a check that one row changed.

drill.prompt: Close this page. Each account gets five free cash withdrawals a month, counted as tokens in an `AtomicInteger`. alt.title: Kotlin

recap: An atomic variable does one read-modify-write as a single step that no thread can split, with `volatile` visibility, and no thread ever waits for another.
`compareAndSet(expected, next)` writes only if the value is still `expected`. Read, decide, CAS, and retry on failure: that loop builds any update.
`updateAndGet` and its relatives contain the loop, so your function may run more than once. Keep it pure.
`LongAdder` beats `AtomicLong` for busy counters, but `sum()` is not a snapshot. Use `AtomicLong` when the value drives a decision.
`AtomicReference` and an immutable object change several fields in one swap. ABA needs reuse; `AtomicStampedReference` catches it.
The limit: one CAS covers one variable, and two atomic calls in a row are not atomic. Put the check inside the CAS.
closing:
We started with eight tellers on one balance and an `AtomicLong` we had taken on trust. Underneath, it was one processor instruction, and for anything bigger, a loop: read, decide, compare-and-set, and decide again on failure. We counted a busy day with a `LongAdder`, and moved money between two balances in one swap.

Now search your own code for an atomic's `get()` followed by another call on the same atomic. An `if (x.get() ...)` before an `x.addAndGet(...)` is check-then-act, built from atomic parts.

Next, we'll open the collections built from these same pieces. What does a `ConcurrentHashMap` really promise when eight tellers write to it at once?

quiz.q: Sixteen threads count every deposit the bank takes. The manager's screen reads the count once a minute. Which is the best fit?
options: A `volatile long` with `count++`
A `synchronized` increment method
An `AtomicLong` with `incrementAndGet()`
A `LongAdder` with `increment()` and `sum()`
quiz.why: Many writers and a rare read that may be a little behind is exactly what `LongAdder` is for: threads mostly update different cells, so they don't fight over one cache line. `AtomicLong` is correct, but slower under this much contention. `synchronized` is correct and slower still. `volatile` with `++` loses deposits.

`getAndIncrement` returns the old value (5) and leaves 6. `incrementAndGet` makes it 7 and returns the new value (7). The final `get()` is 7. The name says the order: get, then increment, or increment, then get.

quiz.q: `balance.updateAndGet(b -> { long next = b - cents; sms.send("New balance: " + next); return next; })` runs on many threads. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: `updateAndGet` runs the function exactly once per call
The balance can lose a withdrawal
Customers can get texts about balances their account never had, because the function runs again whenever its compare-and-set fails
It throws `IllegalStateException` when threads collide
quiz.why: When a compare-and-set fails, `updateAndGet` calls the function again with the fresh value. The failed attempt has already sent its text, with a balance that was never stored. The balance itself is correct, which is why this bug is easy to miss. Keep the function pure, and send the text after the call, with the value it returned.

quiz.q: From synchronized and intrinsic locks: to show the average deposit, the bank keeps `count` and `totalCents` for today's deposits, and both must always change together. Which is a correct choice?
options: Two `AtomicLong` fields, each updated with `addAndGet`
One `AtomicReference` to an immutable record holding both values, or a `synchronized` method that updates both
Two `volatile long` fields
Two `LongAdder` fields
quiz.why: Each atomic protects one variable. With two of them, a reader can see the new count with the old total. One lock around both updates, or one compare-and-set on a reference to an immutable pair, makes the two fields change as one step.

quiz.q: When is ABA a real risk for a compare-and-set in Java?
options: On every `AtomicReference` CAS, even with freshly built nodes
Only on ARM processors
Never: the JVM prevents it
When the same value can come back after changes: recycled nodes, object pools, array indices, plain counters
quiz.why: CAS only checks that the value equals what you read, so it's fooled only if the value can return to an earlier one. With new nodes, the garbage collector won't reuse a node's memory while any thread still holds a reference to it, so it can't come back. Pools, indices and numbers can, and `AtomicStampedReference` adds a version number to catch it.

flashcards.back: As one indivisible step: if the current value equals `expected`, it stores `next` and returns `true`. Otherwise it changes nothing and returns `false`.
`incrementAndGet()` returns the new value. `getAndIncrement()` returns the old value. Both add one atomically.

flashcards.front: Why must the function passed to `updateAndGet` have no side effects?
flashcards.back: When its compare-and-set loses a race, `updateAndGet` calls the function again with the new value. It can run several times for one update.
`LongAdder`: threads update separate cells, so there is far less contention. Use `AtomicLong` when the exact value drives a decision.

flashcards.front: Is `LongAdder.sum()` an exact snapshot while other threads add?
flashcards.back: No. It reads the cells one at a time, so increments made during the sum may be missed.
A CAS succeeds because the value is back to what you read (A, then B, then A again), though it changed in between. Fix it with a version stamp: `AtomicStampedReference`.
No. Two atomic calls with a gap between them is check-then-act. Do the check inside a CAS loop or `updateAndGet`.

terms.plain: A variable whose read-modify-write operations happen as one step that no other thread can split.
Write a new value only if the current value is still the one you expected, and report whether it worked.
Read, decide, try a CAS, and start over if another thread changed the value first.
Some thread always makes progress, even if others are paused, because nobody holds a lock.
Many threads trying to change the same thing at the same moment.
A function that only reads its input and returns a result, with no side effects, so running it twice does no harm.
A counter spread over several cells so threads rarely collide; its sum is not a snapshot.
A CAS that succeeds because a value changed and then changed back.

explain_back.prompt: Explain, in your own words, how a compare-and-set loop can update a shared balance correctly without any thread ever waiting for a lock.
explain_back.answer: Each thread reads the current balance, works out the balance it wants, and then asks the processor to store it only if the variable still holds what it read. That compare-and-set is a single instruction, so no other thread can slip in between the compare and the store. If another thread changed the balance first, the CAS fails and nothing is written, so the thread reads again and decides again from the fresh value. A thread never waits for another; it just retries. Every failed CAS means some other thread succeeded, so the program as a whole always makes progress. The catch is that the work inside the loop may run several times, so it must have no side effects.

sources.title: Java Concurrency in Practice, Goetz et al., chapter 15
